newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO steps up patrols in disputed Bosnian towns.
newsitem.headline: NATO steps up patrols in disputed Bosnian towns.

text.p: NATO said on Sunday that Spanish peacekeeping troops had stepped up patrols in the Bosnian town of Mostar after a spate of explosions raised tensions between rival Moslem and Croat communities.
The NATO-led peace force said it ordered the move to try to discourage further violence which has accompanied political battles between Moslem and Croat leaders, a spokesman said.
"The Spanish are increasing the frequency of patrols to try and calm things down there," Major Tony White, a spokesman for the Stabilisation Force (SFOR) told Reuters.

International police monitors reported an explosion on Saturday afternoon in a main square straddling a former front line. On Friday evening, a blast shattered windows in a Roman Catholic monastery in the Croat-held western sector.
In the worst violence in several months, seven explosions rocked Mostar on Thursday, including two rifle grenades fired at an apartment building.

SFOR has condemned the attacks but says it is up to local police, not peacekeeping troops, to arrest those responsible. The incidents in Mostar fall outside of SFOR's military mission to separate rival armies, NATO commanders say.

The source of the explosions, most of which occurred on the Croat-held western sector of Mostar, remains unknown. But international police officials suspect grenades may have been used in cases where the blasts caused no major material damage.
Croat media, under the strict control of Croat politicians, blamed Moslems in eastern Mostar for the incidents.
Local Moslem leaders appealed for calm and accused "extremists" of launching attacks to halt efforts at reunifying the town.
Moslems and Croats fought a vicious 10-month war in 1993-94 before forming a federation under heavy U.S. pressure. The conflict left Mostar divided into Moslem and Croat sectors.
Croat hardline nationalists refuse to fulfil promises to end the town's partition and have tolerated expulsions of the remaining Moslems in western Mostar.
SFOR had also sent U.S. reinforcements to the northern town of Brcko as a deadline approached for a decision to settle the future status of the area.

An American arbiter must deliver a ruling by February 15 to determine who will control the strategic town, the subject of a long-running territorial dispute which nearly undermined a peace agreement reached in November 1995.
An SFOR officer who asked not to be named said additional U.S. troops were deployed in Serb-held Brcko as a deterrent to any possible violence in the days leading up to the deadline.
"We have made adjustments to our resources over the last month as a precautionary measure and to get a general assessment of the situation," the officer said.

The commander of the U.S. Second Brigade deployed in the Brcko area, Colonel Mike Thompson, obtained pledges from Serb, Croat and Moslem police and government officials to support any decision over Brcko in a meeting last week.
Apart from hostile political rhetoric, Brcko has been calm in the run-up to the deadline, SFOR reported.
